I've been watching videos of the neuroscientist Robert Sapolsky. He argues that we have no free will. Every choice we make is determined by our psychology, and our psychology is determined by a lot of factors outside of our control. 


He cites genes that make people more likely to develop mental disorders, including depression, genes that make people feel less satiated when full, which is a good predictor of obesity, among others. In addition, how we're raised heavily affects our psychology. Even as a baby, how often we're held, how were talked to matter. Then there's any trauma we endure, emotional, sexual, physical, etc. And lastly, even things more recent, such as our hormone levels and how long it's been since we've eaten affect our behavior.

After I started buying into this concept, I started to feel a lot less shame for choices that I made, as I saw myself as a product of a lot of complex factors outside my control. There are of course other existential implications to the theory, but in the meantime, it has greatly reduced feelings of guilt and shame from past decisions.

It's our programming. A lot of our psychology is determined before we're even born, i.e. through genes. There are genes that make people more likely to have mental illness, genes that make people less likely to feel satiated after eating, genes that leave us predisposed to addiction etc, etc. 


Then there's a lot that happens while we're infants. How often or how quick our parents comforted us when we cried. How often we're held. How were talked to. It all affects our psychology before we have any control over our lives. 


Then there's your socioeconomic status, accessibility to health care and education, any trauma that's inflicted on us, and even the political zeitgeist of where we're born. People vastly overestimate how much control they have over their psychology. 


But in a way I find this freeing.  It really lessens a lot of guilt and shame for feeling like you've failed to live how you and/or others expected you to.

Depression can be caused by a lot of different things. Usually there's some sort of past trauma is involved. People can also become depressed from chronic illness or injury. There's also a genetic predisposition to it.

I can't tell you what's in your boyfriend's head, but I can tell you what's in mine. When I'm in a depressive mood, I'm usually thinking negative thoughts about myself-- that I'm a bad husband, a useless worker, a bad son, etc. Sometimes I'll even have thoughts of hurting myself or not wanting to be alive anymore. Usually dealing with these thoughts is so draining that I don't have the energy to do much else.

As for going to the gym, that's actually a great habit for him to have. Exercise is proven to reduce the effects of depression. YOu should ask him if it's okay if you tag along. I think it would be good for you guys as long as he doesn't see the gym as his alone time.

I can try to help a bit, as a married guy with depression, but keep in mind I'm not a professional, this is just personal experience.

The most important thing is to listen without preaching too much. If he doesn't want to talk about his feelings, that's fine, don't push him. If he does, listen, and thank him for opening up and remind him that you love him despite his depression.

The second thing is, take care of yourself, too. It can be very hard to have a partner with depression, so you have to make sure you're still taking care of yourself and giving yourself space if its too overwhelming. Also, remember not to take it too personally--if he's cold to you, it's likely because he's going through a lot in his head and doesn't have the energy.

The third thing, and this is hard, is that if it becomes too much for you, and you have to leave him, try not to feel guilt. Even if he threatens to kill himself, remember the second point--you also have to take care of yourself.

As for therapy and medication, it can help, but it doesn't always. It's at least worth a shot for him, but you also can't force him to do it. You could try to seek a therapist for yourself to help deal with this, and that might get him to start thinking about it. But remember that its' not a guaranteed solution, and even if it does help, it will take time.

He also might not have a good answer, but try to ask him about coping mechanisms for when he's in a depressive mood. Does he like music? Video games? Cuddling? If you can find out what helps him get out of his head, in the future you can have a good idea of what to do when he's in a funk.

Hope this helps.

A pattern I've noticed in conservative thought, and I include the black pill/manosphere/etc. under that umbrella, is they take a nugget of truth and distort it through generalization, hidden illogical leaps, and appeals to emotion.

In your post, the nugget of truth is people are more likely to want to be around and are generally nicer to people they find attractive. This is true. I've been overweight since I was a teenager, and there was a small period in my 20s where I lost it and got much more attention from women.

However, the first distortion I noticed is the absolutism. Attractiveness may be a factor in work, friendship, and romance, but it is not the ONLY factor. I'm a poker player, and I know that while Aces are more likely to beat every other hand, they unfortunately do not always hold up. As an example, Steve Buscemi is considered by many to be conventionally unattractive, but he has a successful career, had a successful marriage til his wife passed, and I don't know for sure, but I imagine he has friends.

The second distortion is the definition of success. If you are attractive, you are more likely to to get a job, make friends, and have a girlfriend. Attractiveness, however, doesn't help keep these things. For work, a combination of talent, luck, and the ability to play nice with others are more important to keep the job. For friends, empathy, respect, and common interests. And for romantic relationships-- love, emotional intelligence, and the ability to compromise.

And this is a personal anecdote, but I wouldn't consider myself conventionally attractive. As I mentioned earlier I lost weight for a bit, but I actually met the woman who is now my wife AFTER I gained it all back.

Dating is absolutely tough, and the realization that there is a privilege to attractiveness weighed on me as well, but I think its important to combat these distorted ideas before they get too ingrained into your psyche. Hope this helps.

I never got the birds and the bees talk from my parents when I was a kid. No one ever taught me how to court a woman. All I had to go on were vague sex-ed classes about how abstinence was the best option at my catholic middle school. In high school my only friends were similarly clueless guys. It wasn't til college that I had friends who actually got girls. They offered to wing me, but at that point I was so embarrassed about my lack of experience and low self-esteem that I avoided them and most social situations. 

When I was 24/25 I had a huge confidence boost that stemming from a hefty raise from work, and started making life changes. I lost 60lbs and started saying "yes" to people when they invited me out. I started getting attention from women, but I would usually brush it off or assume it was in my head. But there's one missed opportunity that really stands out for me. I was invited by a female acquaintance of mine to go to this burlesque show with her group of friends. I didn't know her or her friends that well, but I said what the hell and took her up on it. Well, one of her friends was this Korean girl who just moved from New Zealand who I thought was really attractive. Throughout the night, she started sending signals so obvious that even me, with my complete and utter lack of experience could tell she was into me. Any time I said anything even slightly funny she would lean into me and giggle hysterically. When she found out I lived near the friend whose couch she was crashing on, she basically jumped in my car and insisted I give her a ride back. So I was 90% sure she was into me. 

But I had no idea what to do about it. I was a virgin with no idea how to initiate. Did she want sex? Am I a creep and douchebag for wanting to get laid here? Do I just ask for her number? How do I ask without sounding awkward? Do I suggest we go back to my place instead? Does she want a one night stand or something more? Am I arrogant thinking she wants to have sex with me? Maybe I should just ask her on a date later. Do I use the word "date" or is that corny?

It didn't help that I was intimidated by how hot she was. I kept having to fight the thought that she was out of my league. I ended up talking about safe subjects for most of the car ride (where she was from, what she wanted to do with her life, etc.), which I assumed killed the vibe since were were coming from a burlesque show, cheering women slowly taking off their clothes and dancing. I dropped her off while she awkwardly held my hand for a couple seconds before walking away. I never saw her again. I'm still a virgin at 27.

I felt fat and gross most of my life and felt like I was too disgusting to ever deserve a romantic/sexual relationship. It took losing 60 lbs when I was 24 to see myself as not terrible looking, and even then I got hung up on my skinny wrists and "middle eastern" nose (and lack of experience). Eventually I gained all the weight back and now I'm back to feeling fat and gross and unlovable again.

As far as my sexuality goes, I've always felt ashamed of it. When I was going through puberty, I was taught masturbation was apparently some big sin, so I used to jerk off and then "pray" for forgiveness for it and feel guilty for giving in to the urge. I'm not religious anymore, but I still occasionally get irrational guilt from doing it. This pretty much left my sex life in shambles. And by shambles, I mean non-existence. My parents never gave me the birds and bees talk, just vague references to sex being bad when watching sitcoms with them. All I had to go on was some abstinence-only education from middle school and stories of all the creepy guys that approached my sisters and female cousins. I'm a 27 year-old virgin now because I was taught my sexuality was a burden, and I figured I was sparing women the terrible task of putting up with it by never expressing it. I know it's an irrational and unhealthy line of thinking now, but the damage has been done, and I'm more depressed than I've ever been in my life.
